extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students / readers learning elementary proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked solutions for producing and evaluating elementary mathematical proofs (contradiction, contrapositive, induction, pigeonhole, parity, set/relations/functions) as in Hammack's Book of Proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired statement and derive a contradiction; used to show existence/irrationality/etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show u=r+√2/2 is irrational, assume u is rational and express √2 as a quotient of integers, yielding a contradiction. Structure: assume negation, manipulate algebraically to produce an impossible rational/integer claim, conclude original statement true. Useful for statements about irrationality or impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universal statement false, present a specific counterexample that violates it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Claim 'There exist primes p,q with p−q=97' is false: reason about parity to deduce one must equal 2, then show resulting values are not prime. Simpler: exhibit explicit numbers (e.g., a=6,b=3,c=4) to refute divisibility claims. Provide a concrete counterexample and brief justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove 'if P then Q' by proving the logically equivalent contrapositive 'if not Q then not P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To prove 'If x^2 < y^2 then x < y', take contrapositive 'if x ≥ y then x^2 ≥ y^2' and argue by cases on signs. Label the method (e.g., 'Proof. (Contrapositive)') and handle cases as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis (split into exhaustive cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the proof into mutually exclusive cases (e.g., sign, parity, membership) and prove the statement in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include separating when x and y have opposite signs or not; handling parity (even/odd) in primality/disproof arguments; or treating k values in combinatorial identities. Explicitly state cases and reason within each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (weak)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements about integers by verifying a base case and showing 'if true for k then true for k+1'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard template used throughout: (1) Base case (n=1 or n=0) verified; (2) Inductive step assumes statement for k, derives it for k+1 via algebraic manipulation or factorization. Examples: sums 1+2+...+n, sum of cubes, divisibility statements, binomial theorem (by induction on exponent). Show algebraic steps clearly and close the inductive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the statement holds for all integers up to k and use that to prove it for k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the k+1 case depends on multiple previous cases (e.g., set identities, counting regions determined by lines). Explicitly state the inductive hypothesis 'true for k or fewer sets' and show how it implies the k+1 case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Intermediate Value Theorem for existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke continuity/IVT to assert existence of a real number with a specified property when explicit construction is difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: assert existence of positive m with m^{2^n} = L (used to argue existence of a root). When used, mention the theorem as justification for existence rather than algebraic construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason about even/odd parity to deduce impossibility or to classify cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: primes differing by an odd number must have opposite parity, hence one must be 2; proving 6|(n^3−n) by showing product factors contain even and multiple-of-3 factors; use 'one of k or k+1 is even' in inductive divisibility proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuting universal quantifiers by parity/case contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine parity reasoning with direct contradiction to refute statements that claim existence or divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show no primes p,q satisfy p−q=97 by parity and checking consequences; structure argument by assuming existence and deducing impossible parity-based outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating false implications with counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that an implication or alleged general rule is false by giving specific values that violate the consequent while satisfying the antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show 'if |x+y| = |x−y| then y=0' is false by choosing x=0,y=1; show 'a|bc implies a|b or a|c' is false with a=6,b=3,c=4. Provide explicit substitutions and compute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving reflexive/symmetric/transitive properties of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a relation R has a property, use the definition directly: reflexive (xRx for all x), symmetric (xRy ⇒ yRx), transitive (xRy and yRz ⇒ xRz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show relation xRy iff x−y∈Z is reflexive/symmetric/transitive by algebraic manipulation; for 4|(x+3y) check 3 properties and then compute equivalence classes. Use direct verification with algebraic equations and integer arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing equivalence relations and computing equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: After proving reflexive/symmetric/transitive, determine equivalence classes by solving the defining congruence relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: congruence modulo 2 produces two classes (evens/odds); relation 4|(x+3y) yields four residue classes computed explicitly. Show how to compute [a] = {x: relation holds with a}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving injectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Show f(x)=f(y) implies x=y by algebraic manipulation or logical deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for f(n)=2n+1, assume f(m)=f(n) and deduce m=n; for rational functions solve resulting equation showing uniqueness. Make algebraic steps explicit and justify divisions by nonzero factors when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an arbitrary b in the codomain, construct or solve for x in domain with f(x)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for f(x)=(5x+1)/(x−2) on R\{2} show for arbitrary b≠5 solve x = (−2b−1)/(5−b) and check domain exclusion. Explicitly solve and note nonzero denominators or excluded values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving bijectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish both injectivity and surjectivity (often separately) to conclude bijection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after proving injectivity and surjectivity of f(x)=(5x+1)/(x−2) conclude bijective. State both parts and combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing non-injectivity/non-surjectivity by explicit examples
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a function is not injective, produce two distinct inputs mapping to same output; to show not surjective, produce an element of codomain with no preimage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(0,1)=f(0,0) for f(x,y)=(xy,x^2) shows non-injectivity; constant-output functions show non-surjectivity. Provide explicit pairs and compute outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (partition-and-count proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the domain into finitely many pigeonholes; if more pigeons than holes, two must share a hole leading to the desired conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: among 6 integers two share same remainder mod 5; among 7 naturals there exist two whose sum or difference divisible by 10 by constructing 12 candidate sums/differences and 10 last-digit classes. Explicitly define partition and show |pigeons|>|holes|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility via algebraic factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove divisibility by factoring expressions to exhibit a factor multiplied by an integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show 24|(5^{2^{n}}−1) by writing 5^{2^{k+1}}−1 = 25(5^{2^k})−1 = 24(25a+1) given previous step; show n^3−n factors as n(n−1)(n+1) to prove divisibility by 6. Use algebraic identities and integer multiple arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Pascal's identity and combinatorial identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Pascal's formula (n choose k) = (n−1 choose k)+(n−1 choose k−1) and related identities in combinatorial proofs and in induction steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: induction proof of binomial theorem and many binomial sum identities use Pascal's identity repeatedly and combine inductive hypothesis. Quote Pascal when expanding binomial sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting arguments using the multiplication principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Count structures by multiplying choices for independent components to enumerate functions, relations, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of functions from 7-element set to 7-element set is 7^7; number of injective functions is 7!. Use multiplication principle and explain independence of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set identities by element-chasing and laws (De Morgan, distributive)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove set equalities, pick an arbitrary element and show membership equivalence using definitions and set laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show complement of intersection equals union of complements by writing x∈A^c∩B^c iff not(x∈A∩B) and applying De Morgan. Explicitly use definitions and logical equivalences step-by-step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform algebraic expressions to compare / bound quantities (inequalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulate algebraic sums/products to derive inequalities or demonstrate bounds (often within induction proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prove sum_{k=1}^n 1/k < 2 by pairing terms and using inductive decomposition; or show polynomial inequalities by expanding and collecting terms. Make each inequality step explicit and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with modular arithmetic and residue classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe equivalence classes modulo n, compute addition/multiplication tables, and use congruence properties in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: list partitions of Z by residues mod 4; show [a][b]=[0] implies one factor [0] in Z_5 by inspecting multiplication table. Present representatives and arithmetic tables when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using explicit algebraic manipulation for function composition
rubrics_metrics.description: When composing functions, compute gof and fog explicitly by substituting formulas and simplifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: compute g∘f and f∘g for given formulas f(x)=√(x+1), g(x)=x^4 or for functions on Z×Z by substitution; show resulting expressions and note differences (non-commutativity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling proof method and structuring exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly indicate the proof technique (e.g., 'Proof. (Outline)', 'Proof. (Contrapositive)') and structure the argument with numbered steps or case labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the solutions, methods are labeled and proofs are presented in clear steps (1), (2), etc. Follow this clear structure: state the technique, give base/case/assumption, perform algebra/logic, conclude with 'Thus the result follows' or similar.
